title: Ecological economics

definition.text: A field of research, drawing on many disciplines, that studies how human economies and natural ecosystems depend on each other and change together over time and space.

facts.text: It treats the economy as a subsystem of Earth's larger ecosystem and stresses keeping natural capital intact, which sets it apart from mainstream environmental economics.
Ecological economists favour strong sustainability and reject the idea that human-made capital can stand in for natural capital.
A main aim is to ground economic thinking in physical reality, especially the laws of thermodynamics and knowledge of living systems.
Besides efficient allocation, it puts weight on two further problems: fair distribution, and the size of the economy relative to the ecosystems it relies on.
Where mainstream economists tend to be technological optimists, ecological economists lean towards scepticism and favour precaution, since destroying key environmental resources may be irreversible.
Its topics include weak versus strong sustainability, energy economics and energy accounting, environmental services, cost shifting, modelling and monetary policy.
Economist Malte Faber describes the field as defined by its focus on nature, justice and time.
It was founded as a modern discipline in the 1980s through the work of European and American academics.

notes: Wants the flow diagram replacing the circular flow of income (S:53a741358ee6).

title: Source and sink functions of the environment

definition.text: The two roles the environment plays for an economy: supplying materials and services (source) and absorbing and neutralising waste and pollution (sink).

facts.text: Ecological economics replaces the simple circular flow of income with a flow diagram in which solar energy sustains natural inputs and services used in production.
Once consumed, natural inputs leave the economy as pollution and waste.
The source function is run down as resources are used up or polluted.
When waste exceeds what the sink can absorb, long-term damage follows; some persistent pollutants such as nuclear waste are absorbed very slowly or not at all.

distinct_from: Costanza's valuation of the global ecosystem

title: Costanza's valuation of the global ecosystem

definition.text: A 1997 study led by Robert Costanza that tried to put a total money value on the services the world's ecosystems provide.

facts.text: Published in Nature, it arrived at $33 trillion, with a range of $16 trillion to $54 trillion, when total global GDP in 1997 was $27 trillion.
Half of the value came from nutrient cycling; estuaries, swamps and floodplains, and seagrass and algae beds had the highest values per hectare.
It averaged values from studies done in very specific settings and transferred them without regard to that setting.
Critics in the journal Ecological Economics still granted that valuing the global ecosystem had positive potential.

distinct_from: Source and sink functions of the environment

definition.text: The distinction ecological economics draws between growth, a quantitative rise in economic output, and development, a qualitative improvement in quality of life.

facts.text: Ecological economists argue that neoclassical economics confuses growth with development.
Beyond modest levels, higher consumption per person may not raise well-being and may harm the environment and society.
Growth of this harmful kind is sometimes called uneconomic growth.
Well-being in ecological economics is distinguished from the welfare concept used in mainstream and environmental economics.

title: Cost shifting

definition.text: The ecological-economics view that environmental and social harms are not occasional side effects ('externalities') but costs that businesses routinely shift onto others.

facts.text: Karl William Kapp's work explains why calling these harms 'externalities' is a misnomer: modern business makes profit by shifting costs onto others as normal practice.
Clive Spash notes that externality theory wrongly treats environmental and social problems as small exceptions in an otherwise efficient system.
On this view, internalising an odd externality does nothing about the structural problem.
Joan Martinez Alier points out that most affected consumers are future generations, who cannot influence today's prices.
By contrast, Paul Hawken argues that unsustainable goods are cheaper only because of a hidden subsidy paid by the environment, communities or future generations.

contested_note: Ecological economists dispute the mainstream view that harms can be corrected by internalising externalities.

title: Critique of ecosystem service valuation

definition.text: The argument, made by Douglas McCauley among others, that putting money values on nature and its services can harm conservation.

facts.text: Not all ecosystem services are financially beneficial: mangroves protect coasts, but wolves hunt cattle.

Money values tie conservation to fluctuating markets: bee pollination near a Costa Rican farm was valued at over US$60,000 a year until coffee prices fell and the fields were replanted with pineapple, which needs no bees.
Human ingenuity can replace ecosystem services by artificial means, which also lowers their value.
Conserving an ecosystem is not always more profitable than altering it, as local fish trade after the Nile perch was introduced to Lake Victoria shows.
McCauley concludes that campaigns should appeal to morality rather than money.

related: Costanza's valuation of the global ecosystem
contested_note: Monetary valuation of nature is widely accepted among ecologists and conservationists, but some argue it is inherently false.

definition.text: How ecological economics grew from 19th-century and early 20th-century ideas into a discipline with its own society and journal by 1989.

facts.text: Its roots go back to the 19th-century Romantics, Malthus's worries about population and Mill's hope for a stationary state.
Frederick Soddy's 1926 book criticised the idea of the economy as a perpetual motion machine able to create infinite wealth.
Georgescu-Roegen's The Entropy Law and the Economic Process (1971) gave the field a framework based on material and energy flows.
The first organised meetings began in 1982 in Sweden; the field was formally founded in 1988 after a series of conferences.
In 1989 the International Society for Ecological Economics was founded and began publishing the journal Ecological Economics, with Robert Costanza as first president and editor.
The main founders were Herman Daly and Robert Costanza from the US, AnnMari Jansson from Sweden and Juan Martínez-Alier from Spain.

definition.text: The competing camps within ecological economics, from those close to mainstream resource economics to far more heterodox ones.

facts.text: Clive Spash sorts environmental work into three groups: new resource economists, new environmental pragmatists and radical social ecological economists.
Degrowth is a growing radical strand that addresses biophysical limits and global inequality.
Critics of degrowth among new resource economists point instead to the momentum of sustainable development and the green economy.

title: Non-western approaches to ecological economics
article: Ecological economics#Non-traditional approaches to ecological economics

definition.text: Cultural and traditional economic outlooks, such as Buen Vivir and Ecological Swaraj, that stress harmony with nature and are now counted as ecological economic practice.

facts.text: Buen Vivir ('Good Life') is a South American movement that rejects the western development model and does not value material accumulation.
Ecological Swaraj, from India, respects physical limits and non-human species and pursues equity through direct democracy.
Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful brought non-western ideas such as Buddhist economics into mainstream thought.

definition.text: An economy that is low-carbon, efficient in its use of resources and socially inclusive; green economics is a more politically applied relative of ecological economics.

facts.text: The idea grew in policy circles first as a response to financial crisis and then as a vehicle for growth and development.
UNEP's definition was developed further in 2011 to stress a fair shift to a low-carbon, resource-efficient, socially inclusive economy.
It looks to cleaner, resource-saving technologies that cut emissions while addressing resource exhaustion.

definition.text: The use of mathematical models to analyse how economies and ecosystems interact.

facts.text: Approaches include evolutionary, input-output, entropy and thermodynamic, multi-criteria and agent-based models, the environmental Kuznets curve and stock-flow consistent frameworks.
System dynamics and GIS are used for spatial simulation of changing landscapes.

definition.text: Ecological economics' work on money and monetary policy, aimed at sustainable scale, just distribution and efficient allocation.

facts.text: This work can be traced to Frederick Soddy's writing on money.
It asks whether interest-bearing debt forces growth, what money is, and whether alternatives such as alternative currencies and public banking would help.

definition.text: Tracking energy into and out of a system, the useful work done and the energy lost, to judge resource use and environmental impact.

facts.text: An energy balance uses the first and second laws of thermodynamics to show how much energy each point in a system needs and in what form.
A key idea is net energy gain: every energy source needs an initial energy investment, so its energy return must exceed one to be useful.
The net energy gain from coal, oil and gas has fallen over time as the easiest sources were depleted first.

definition.text: An economy with a constant stock of physical wealth (capital) and a constant population, so that it does not grow over time.

facts.text: Herman Daly's version keeps both stocks constant by a flow of natural resources through the system; that flow is the new ecological element added to the classical stationary state.
Both stocks should be as durable as possible: longer-lasting capital needs a smaller resource flow, and a durable population has long lives with low birth and death rates.
It rests on the view that the economy is an open subsystem of a finite, non-growing ecosystem, and must therefore itself stop growing at some point.
This contrasts with the mainstream picture of a closed circular flow between firms and households with no physical contact with nature.
Since the 1970s the idea has been linked mainly with Herman Daly.
It can apply to a city, region, country or the whole world.
Daly concedes that a steady state only postpones, not prevents, eventual exhaustion of minerals.
Sympathetic reviewers in the early 2010s judged it beyond what is politically feasible for now.

title: Stationary state in classical economics
article: Steady-state economy#Concept of the stationary state in classical economics

definition.text: The classical economists' idea that an economy would eventually stop growing and settle with a constant population and stock of capital.

facts.text: Classical economists contrasted scarce farmland with growing population and capital.
Capital accumulation would end once the rate of profit fell to a minimum or zero.
Adam Smith believed every national economy would sooner or later reach stationarity.
Unlike Smith and Ricardo, John Stuart Mill was optimistic about the stationary state, making what has been called a quality-of-life argument for it.

title: Daly's institutions for a steady state
article: Steady-state economy#Herman Daly's concept of a steady-state economy

definition.text: Herman Daly's proposal to create a steady-state economy by policy, through three state institutions limiting inequality, population and resource use.

facts.text: The first sets minimum and maximum incomes and a maximum on wealth.
The second issues transferable reproduction licences at the replacement fertility level.
The third sells depletion quotas that cap the flow of resources; unlike taxes, quotas directly minimise throughput.
Daly calls mainstream faith that prices and technology can overcome any scarcity 'growthmania'.

title: Solar-income budget
article: Steady-state economy#Herman Daly's concept of a steady-state economy

definition.text: Daly's term for the limit humans lived within before industrialisation, relying on the steady flow of sunlight rather than the stock of minerals.

facts.text: Daly sees two sources of wealth: a stock of minerals, which we can extract as fast as we choose, and a flow of solar energy beyond our control.
Because the Sun will keep shining for billions of years, the mineral stock is the crucial scarcity.
The Industrial Revolution broke the budget by extracting minerals at a rapidly increasing rate.

distinct_from: Daly's institutions for a steady state

title: Entropy pessimism

definition.text: The view that technology cannot escape the laws of physics, since every technology turns valuable resources into waste and so raises entropy.

facts.text: Neoclassical production functions treat technology as a factor of production with no mention of natural resource inputs.
In ecological economics, technology is the way natural resources are transformed in production.
Robert Solow replied in 1997 that 'elementary physics' had not by itself prevented growth in industrialised countries.

contested_note: Economists disagree on whether technology can overcome natural resource limits.

definition.text: Four works published between 1966 and 1972 on the importance of natural resources and the environment that led to ecological economics.

facts.text: Boulding's 1966 essay on Spaceship Earth argued that the economy must fit a closed, cyclical system.
Georgescu-Roegen's 1971 book argued that all natural resources are irreversibly degraded when used.
Howard T. Odum's 1971 Environment, Power and Society proposed the maximum power principle.
The Limits to Growth (1972) projected that output, food per person and population would peak and then decline.

title: Declining-state economy

definition.text: The argument, from Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen and degrowth thinkers, that a shrinking economy is better than a steady one for stretching finite minerals.

facts.text: Georgescu-Roegen argued Earth's carrying capacity will fall as finite minerals are extracted, so the world economy heads for collapse.
He proposed a 'minimal bioeconomic program' with restrictions stricter than Daly's.
Daly accepts a declining path but sees the steady state as the necessary first step: an economy must stop before it can reverse.
Rifkin, Latouche and Kerschner argue for declining-state strategies.

contested_note: Steady-state and degrowth advocates disagree whether the economy should stabilise or shrink.

title: Degrowth as a path to the steady state

definition.text: Christian Kerschner's view that rich countries should shrink their economies as a route to a fair world steady-state economy.

facts.text: Shrinking rich economies would leave ecological room for poorer countries to catch up.
Kerschner admits a world steady state may stay out of reach but says such goals can guide action.
Two comparative studies found no analytical difference between Daly's steady-state economics and European degrowth.

title: Capitalism without growth

definition.text: The question, raised by radical critics, of whether a steady or shrinking economy can be imposed on top of capitalism.

facts.text: Critics point to growth drives built into capitalism: the profit motive, jobs that depend on sales, credit creation by banks and labour-saving technology.
Governments need tax revenue from economic activity, and globalisation forces countries to compete.
Daly holds that the growth versus steady-state debate cuts across the left-right divide.

contested_note: Radical critics doubt a non-growing capitalism is possible; Daly argues the question cuts across left and right.

title: Resource decoupling
article: Steady-state economy#Resource decoupling and the rebound effect

definition.text: Economic activity becoming less demanding on nature, so fewer natural resources are needed per unit of output.

facts.text: It is measured by the ratio of total natural resource consumption to GDP.
Relative decoupling is a decline in resource use with all else equal; absolute decoupling is a decline in resource use while GDP keeps growing.
A 2019 review found that attempts to grow without environmental destruction had not succeeded.

title: Overdevelopment
article: Steady-state economy#The concept of Overdevelopment by Leopold Cohr

definition.text: The idea that rich countries of the global north are too developed, increasing humanity's ecological impact and causing problems for both rich and poor countries.

facts.text: It is based on Leopold Kohr's 1977 book The Overdeveloped Nations, mainly about overconsumption.

title: Space colonisation and limits to growth
article: Steady-state economy#Pushing some of the terrestrial limits into outer space

definition.text: The proposal that settling outer space could ease overpopulation and resource limits on Earth.

facts.text: In the 1970s Gerard K. O'Neill planned space settlements to solve overpopulation and limits to growth without political repression.

title: Great Stagnation critique of degrowth

definition.text: Wim Naudé's criticism that Western economies already resemble degrowth, in a 'Great Stagnation' of falling innovation and entrepreneurship.

facts.text: In prolonged stagnation, the economy increasingly works like a zero-sum system.

contested_note: Naudé's critique disputes the benefits claimed for degrowth and the steady state.
